note: THE CARD THAT PROVES THE MALE CONSTANT IS ACTIVELY WRONG AND NOT MERELY LIMITING, and it is now measured rather than argued. Without base_tags, compose.py:1482 appends 'male focus, mature male, masculine' to a nine-year-old. With base_tags carrying 'child focus, young boy, small' - plus 'adult, mature male, muscular, tall' pushed into the NEGATIVE at render time - the sheet, all 16 turnaround views and all six sweep cells render an unmistakable nine-year-old. The negative half of that fix is NOT reachable from this card; see the renderer defect noted on NIKA. | PARTLY CORRECTED 2026-08-04. short.py now writes node 6 and drops any negative clause the positive is asking for, so the gender contradiction is gone for NIKA. IT DOES NOTHING FOR PIP, and that is the honest state: his positive contains none of the shipped negative's words, so his negative comes back byte-identical. What he actually needs is 'adult, mature male, muscular, tall' pushed INTO the negative, and no card field can express that. The renderer will not invent it. A `negative_add` field on the character card, assembled by compose and appended by short.py, is the remaining work. | ALSO FIXED 2026-08-04: `lora_strength_measured` now reaches the renderer - compile.py emits character_lora_weights, short.py reads it, and a beat of his loads at 0.5 instead of the old hard 0.85 default. | HIS DAMAGE LADDER IS MUD, NOT BLOOD, because the WEAR fallback ends at 'torn bloodied uniform, cut on face' and that is a different film. | THE HELD PROP SURVIVES, AND TRAINING IMPROVES IT. This was the open question - memory records that a style named after an object gets the object drawn, but not whether a prop SURVIVES a turnaround. It does. The dinosaur is present in most of the 16 views and in every sweep cell. Better than that: WITHOUT the LoRA the prop is unreliable - the control cells render a shapeless green blob in one scene and a BLUE DOLPHIN in the other - while at 0.85 it is an unmistakable green spiky dinosaur in both. The LoRA learned the prop as part of the character. | A HIGHLIGHT IN THE SHEET BECAME PERMANENT TWO-TONE HAIR. His sheet rendered white/silver tufts at the crown; the qwen turnaround amplified them into every one of the 16 views (the 'back' view reads almost entirely white), so the LoRA learned white-over-orange as his hair. It is clearly visible at 0.85 in the sweep. THIS IS THE SECOND TIME THIS HAS HAPPENED IN THIS PROJECT - VIRO's card asks for 'long dark brown curly hair' and character-viro.json's verdict describes pale blond over the crown falling to dark brown as an identity feature. A stray highlight in a one-off sheet becomes a permanent character trait, because the turnaround treats the sheet as ground truth and the LoRA treats the turnaround as ground truth. CHECK THE SHEET BEFORE TURNING IT AROUND. | THE ODD BOOTS NEVER HELD. 'one red rubber boot, one green rubber boot' is in every rung of the ladder. The sheet is framed upper-body so they never appeared in it, the turnaround's full_body view gave him plain brown boots, and the sweep gives red+green once, both-green twice and yellow+green twice. Nothing holds them, LoRA or not. A detail below the frame of the reference sheet cannot be trained in. | VOICE CAVEAT: belinda is the only child voice in the library and it is a young girl. NOT verified by listening. | `prose` is the VISUAL description used by the qwen engine; `desc` is narrative and tells an image model nothing it can draw.
lora_verdict: MEASURED by looking at studio/samples/cast/pip_sweep.jpg - two scenes, three strengths, one seed per row. WHAT IT ADDS: the toy dinosaur becomes an actual dinosaur rather than a blob or a dolphin, the face and freckles lock, and the raincoat silhouette matches the sheet. Neither undertrained (the control differs plainly) nor overfit (every cell is a new scene at a new framing). WHAT IT COSTS: the background, but MUCH less than NIKA's does, and the difference is the useful finding. At 0.85 PIP's neon street washes to a hazy beige with the crowd reduced to outlines, and his sunlit field pales to a flat gradient - degraded but still recognisably the scene. NIKA's field at the same strength collapses to a dark grey void. THE LoRA DRAGS ITS OWN TRAINING BACKGROUND'S VALUE AND HUE, so the damage depends on how far the target scene sits from it: PIP was trained on a light warm grey and merely pales a bright scene, NIKA was trained on a dark blue-grey and destroys one. That refines the project's existing note, which recorded the cost without explaining why it varies. USE 0.5 for scene work; 0.85 is defensible for PIP alone if the prop matters more than the setting, and it also bakes in the white hair tuft.
